title: Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES)
lead: This chapter is mainly about recognition and fast referral. The physiotherapist does not treat CES. The physiotherapist identifies it and sends the patient to hospital without delay.
case: Case: A 34-year-old woman has 5 days of low back pain and right leg pain. She mentions that urine has been harder to start for 2 days and she did not feel the toilet paper when wiping. Left leg feels heavy. Reflexes appear slightly reduced at the ankles. She says it is probably stress.
Decision: suspected CES. Stop the session, explain the concern simply, arrange emergency hospital transfer the same day, give the clinician a written summary, and document time and actions.

differentials.name: Unilateral lumbar radiculopathy
differentials.key: One leg, no bladder or saddle symptoms

differentials.name: Urinary tract infection or prostate problem
differentials.key: Burning urine, frequency, no saddle numbness, normal neurology
differentials.next: Medical review. If neurology is abnormal, treat as CES until excluded

differentials.name: Spinal cord conus lesion
differentials.key: Both upper motor and lower motor signs, earlier bladder signs

differentials.name: Anxiety or functional symptoms
differentials.next: Do not assume. Exclude CES first

qa: The patient can still pass urine. Is CES excluded? No. CES can start with altered sensation and difficulty starting or weak flow before retention occurs. The early stage is the best time to act.
Why not wait one day to see whether symptoms settle? Delay is linked to worse outcomes and the damage may be permanent.
The patient is embarrassed and asks you not to refer. What do you do? Explain calmly why it is important, check that they understand, and refer. Respect their feelings, but the safety risk is high.
Why ask about bladder and saddle symptoms every time, not only on the first visit? CES can develop after the first assessment, for example after a disc herniation enlarges.
Normal reflexes and strong legs but saddle numbness. What now? Emergency referral. Saddle numbness alone is enough reason to act.

redFlags.Immediate action: Stop treatment; send to emergency department the same day, state suspected CES clearly

redFlags.Finding: New sexual dysfunction with back pain
Bilateral or rapidly progressive leg weakness

manualNotes: Not applicable before diagnosis and surgical review. Do not apply them to a patient with suspected CES. After surgery, treatment follows the surgeon's instruction (see L).
pathway: Does the patient report any of: saddle numbness, new bladder or bowel change, new sexual dysfunction, or bilateral progressive leg symptoms? Yes: emergency referral now.
No: continue the relevant pathway and re-screen at every visit.
If unsure: refer, and explain the reason in the referral note.

Hospital phase: usually urgent imaging and a decision about decompression surgery by the medical team. Earlier decompression is generally associated with better outcomes, but exact timing guidance varies.
Rehabilitation after surgery or conservative medical care: a team approach including a physician, nurse, continence specialist, pelvic health physiotherapist and occupational therapist.

Physiotherapy goals: safe walking, strength recovery for the affected muscles, balance, falls prevention, pain management, education about bladder and bowel routines (guided by the specialist team), pelvic floor referral, and return to function.
Long-term support: some patients keep bladder, bowel, sexual or pain problems. Psychological support and peer information are important.
